1: # Bookmark Manager
2: 
3: ## Overview
4: 
5: A **Bookmark Manager** is a personal library application for the web: it saves references to web resources as durable records, organizes them under the user's control, and makes them findable later so the user can return to those resources.
6: 
7: The defining core is small:
8: 
9: ```text
10: Deliberately saved reference record
11: └── anchored to an external web resource by its address (URL)
12:     └── held in a persistent, accumulating personal library
13:         └── under user-controlled organization
14:             └── retrieved later to return to the resource
15: ```
16: 
17: Everything else commonly associated with the category — browser extensions, automatic metadata, tags and nested collections, cloud sync, duplicate and broken-link management, preserved copies of pages, public sharing — is standard equipment of mature modern products rather than what makes the product a bookmark manager. Older and platform-native forms of the same idea (a browser's built-in bookmark folders, the tag-only social bookmarking services of the mid-2000s) satisfy the core without any of those features.
18: 
19: The essential job is **save now, find later**. When the center of gravity shifts to consuming captured content (a reading queue), publishing collections for an audience, or storing user-authored material, the product is drifting toward a different Application Type (Read-it-later, Content Curation, or Note-taking respectively).
20: 
21: ## Users & Context
22: 
23: The primary user is an individual who encounters web resources faster than they can act on them: articles, tools, documentation, references, inspiration, things to buy, things to revisit. They save deliberately — each record exists because the person chose to keep that page — and return weeks, months, or years later.
24: 
25: Typical reasons to open the application:
26: 
27: - save a page just encountered, in one click, without losing browsing flow
28: - put a saved page where it belongs (topic, project, list)
29: - find "that page I saw a while ago" by remembering a word, a tag, or roughly where it was filed
30: - return to a specific known resource (a tool, a reference, a recipe) instead of searching the web for it again
31: - clean house: remove dead links, merge duplicates, restructure
32: 
33: Secondary contexts: small teams or groups maintaining shared collections (research, reading lists, project links); public sharing of a curated list when the owner chooses to. The work environment is inherently multi-device — the whole point of a standalone library is that it is not trapped in one browser or one machine.
34: 
35: ## Core Model
36: 
37: ### The Defining Core
38: 
39: Four properties. If any one is removed, the product is no longer recognizable as a bookmark manager:
40: 
41: - **Reference record anchored to an address** — the central object is a record that points at a web resource via its URL, enriched with whatever metadata the product adds. The record is not the content; the content lives on the web, outside the library. This is what separates the Type from notes (authored content) and from read-it-later services (the captured readable copy is the working object).
42: - **Deliberate capture** — every record originates from a user decision to save (a click, a share, a pasted URL, an approved import). Nothing is logged automatically. This is what separates the library from browser history.
43: - **Persistent, accumulating personal library** — records survive sessions and devices and pile up over time into a long-lived personal asset, often numbering thousands of items.
44: - **User-controlled organization and retrieval** — the user structures the library in some form and can find records again by browsing that structure and/or by searching. The *form* of organization is an implementation choice, not part of the definition.
45: 
46: ### The Record
47: 
48: A bookmark record typically carries:
49: 
50: - the resource's URL — the anchor and, in most products, the record's identity
51: - title and description (fetched from the page automatically in many modern products, and user-editable everywhere)
52: - a preview thumbnail or icon
53: - organizational assignments: collections/folders and/or tags
54: - timestamps, favorite/pinned flags, and free-form notes in many products
55: 
56: Concept versus implementation — the core concepts are realized differently across products:
57: 
58: ```text
59: Concept:             Saved reference record
60: Implementations:     link with metadata (universal); record plus preserved page copy;
61:                      uploaded file kept as a library item (some products)
62: 
63: Concept:             User-controlled organization
64: Implementations:     hierarchical folders/collections; tags; favorites/pins;
65:                      manual ordering; an "unsorted" inbox for uncategorized saves
66: 
67: Concept:             Retrieval
68: Implementations:     search over titles/URLs/descriptions/tags (full-text over page
69:                      content in some products); browse by collection or tag; filters; sort
70: ```
71: 
72: ### Capabilities Shared by Mature Products
73: 
74: These are standard in current standalone products. They make the library practical but do not define the Type:
75: 
76: - **Capture machinery** — a browser extension or bookmarklet (save from any page without leaving it), a mobile share-sheet target, a manual "add URL" form, and bulk import from browsers or other services.
77: - **Metadata enrichment** — automatic extraction of title, description, and preview imagery from the saved page; editable by the user.
78: - **Layered organization** — nested collections/folders and/or tags, often both; favorites or pinned items; a landing zone (unsorted/inbox) for saves the user hasn't classified yet.
79: - **Retrieval machinery** — search across the library, filters (by tag, type, date), sorting (newest-first is the common default), and bulk edit tools for reorganizing at scale.
80: - **Multi-device, multi-browser access** — web, desktop, and mobile clients sharing one library; independence from any single browser profile is the reason standalone products exist.
81: - **Interoperability** — import/export in the standard browser-bookmark HTML format, which functions as the Type's interchange convention.
82: - **Library hygiene** — duplicate detection or prevention; awareness of broken links (detection or error listings). Common in standalone products, though depth varies.
83: - **Preservation copies** — a saved snapshot of the page (local file, vendor-hosted copy, or a third-party web archive) so the content survives even if the original disappears. Common in dedicated standalone products; absent from the Type's older and platform-native forms, and therefore not part of the definition.
84: - **Private-first sharing** — the library defaults to private; sharing a single link, a collection, or the whole account is an explicit, optional act.
85: - **Read-later affordances** — unread flags, clean reader views, reminders. A common hybrid overlap with Read-it-later, not part of the definition.
86: 
87: ## How It Works
88: 
89: ### Capture
90: 
91: ```text
92: Encounter a page (in a browser or app)
93: → invoke the save surface (extension / share sheet / add form)
94: → the product creates a record: URL + fetched title, description, preview
95: → optionally pick a collection and add tags at save time
96: → done — the record is in the library
97: ```
98: 
99: Capture is designed to cost seconds. If the user skips classification, the record lands in an unsorted area to be triaged later. Bulk capture exists in both directions: import brings an existing bookmark file or another service's library in at once, and some products can capture all open browser tabs in one action.
100: 
101: ### Organize
102: 
103: ```text
104: Open the unsorted area (or any collection)
105: → assign records to collections, apply or clean up tags
106: → restructure: nest, rename, merge, or reorder collections
107: → bulk operations move or relabel many records at once
108: ```
109: 
110: Organization is retroactive and continuously editable — records can be re-filed at any time, and the organizational structure itself (unlike a file system) is usually cheap to reshape because records are small.
111: 
112: ### Find and return
113: 
114: ```text
115: Remember something about the record (a word, a tag, the topic)
116: → search, or browse to the collection/tag
117: → scan result list (newest-first, or filtered/sorted)
118: → open the record → click through to the live resource
119: ```
120: 
121: Retrieval is the loop the whole Type exists for. Results are the user's own records; the product finds things the user has already seen and chosen to keep — the inverse of a search engine, which finds things the user has never seen.
122: 
123: ### Maintain
124: 
125: ```text
126: Periodically: run duplicate review → merge or remove
127: → check broken-link reports → repair (find replacement) or delete
128: → optionally trigger/request preserved copies of important records
129: → deleted records go to a recoverable trash in some products
130: ```
131: 
132: Because the referenced content lives on the web and out of the application's control, maintenance is a permanent background concern of this Type — link rot is structural, not an edge case.
133: 
134: ## Interfaces
135: 
136: ### Library list (home)
137: 
138: The primary surface: the accumulated records in a browsable list.
139: 
140: - typical information: title, URL/source, thumbnail, tags, collection, date added
141: - primary actions: open record, edit, move, tag, favorite, delete, select-many for bulk actions
142: 
143: ### Capture surface
144: 
145: A small overlay, not a full screen: the browser-extension popup, the mobile share target, or the add form.
146: 
147: - typical information: page URL and fetched title/preview
148: - primary actions: save, pick collection, add tags, (sometimes) set reminder
149: 
150: ### Collection / organization sidebar
151: 
152: The library's structural map.
153: 
154: - typical information: collection tree (often nestable), tag list or cloud, special views (unsorted, favorites, trash)
155: - primary actions: create/rename/nest/merge/delete collections, browse into one
156: 
157: ### Record detail / edit
158: 
159: One record's full surface.
160: 
161: - typical information: URL, title, description, preview, notes, tags, collection, timestamps; sometimes the preserved copy or an embedded reader view
162: - primary actions: edit fields, move/recategorize, open original, preserve copy, delete
163: 
164: ### Search and filters
165: 
166: - typical information: query field, filter controls (tag, type, date), result list
167: - primary actions: search, refine, act on results
168: 
169: ### Trash
170: 
171: Where deletions land in products that offer recovery; excluded from search and normal views until restored or purged.
172: 
173: ## Important Rules / Behaviors
174: 
175: - **The record points; the web owns the content.** A saved page can change or vanish without the record knowing. The library guarantees the *reference*, not the *content* — unless the product also stores a preserved copy, which is an optional capability.
176: - **The library grows only by user action.** Capture is deliberate. Imports and automated intake (e.g., configured feeds) enlarge the library only because the user set them up. There is no silent accumulation as with browser history.
177: - **Organization is user-controlled and always revisable.** No structure is imposed by the system; tags and collections mean what the user wants them to mean, and records can be re-filed indefinitely.

1: # Bookmark Manager
2: 
3: ## Overview
4: 
5: A **Bookmark Manager** is a personal library application for the web: it saves references to web resources as durable records, organizes them under the user's control, and makes them findable later so the user can return to those resources.
6: 
7: The defining core is small:
8: 
9: ```text
10: Deliberately saved reference record
11: └── anchored to an external web resource by its address (URL)
12:     └── held in a persistent, accumulating personal library
13:         └── under user-controlled organization
14:             └── retrieved later to return to the resource
15: ```
16: 
17: Everything else commonly associated with the category — browser extensions, automatic metadata, tags and nested collections, cloud sync, duplicate and broken-link management, preserved copies of pages, public sharing — is standard equipment of mature modern products rather than what makes the product a bookmark manager. Older and platform-native forms of the same idea (a browser's built-in bookmark folders, the tag-only social bookmarking services of the mid-2000s) satisfy the core without any of those features.
18: 
19: The essential job is **save now, find later**. When the center of gravity shifts to consuming captured content (a reading queue), publishing collections for an audience, or storing user-authored material, the product is drifting toward a different Application Type (Read-it-later, Content Curation, or Note-taking respectively).
20: 
21: ## Users & Context
22: 
23: The primary user is an individual who encounters web resources faster than they can act on them: articles, tools, documentation, references, inspiration, things to buy, things to revisit. They save deliberately — each record exists because the person chose to keep that page — and return weeks, months, or years later.
24: 
25: Typical reasons to open the application:
26: 
27: - save a page just encountered, in one click, without losing browsing flow
28: - put a saved page where it belongs (topic, project, list)
29: - find "that page I saw a while ago" by remembering a word, a tag, or roughly where it was filed
30: - return to a specific known resource (a tool, a reference, a recipe) instead of searching the web for it again
31: - clean house: remove dead links, merge duplicates, restructure
32: 
33: Secondary contexts: small teams or groups maintaining shared collections (research, reading lists, project links); public sharing of a curated list when the owner chooses to. The work environment is inherently multi-device — the whole point of a standalone library is that it is not trapped in one browser or one machine.
34: 
35: ## Core Model
36: 
37: ### The Defining Core
38: 
39: Four properties. If any one is removed, the product is no longer recognizable as a bookmark manager:
40: 
41: - **Reference record anchored to an address** — the central object is a record that points at a web resource via its URL, enriched with whatever metadata the product adds. The record is not the content; the content lives on the web, outside the library. This is what separates the Type from notes (authored content) and from read-it-later services (the captured readable copy is the working object).
42: - **Deliberate capture** — every record originates from a user decision to save (a click, a share, a pasted URL, an approved import). Nothing is logged automatically. This is what separates the library from browser history.
43: - **Persistent, accumulating personal library** — records survive sessions and devices and pile up over time into a long-lived personal asset, often numbering thousands of items.
44: - **User-controlled organization and retrieval** — the user structures the library in some form and can find records again by browsing that structure and/or by searching. The *form* of organization is an implementation choice, not part of the definition.
45: 
46: ### The Record
47: 
48: A bookmark record typically carries:
49: 
50: - the resource's URL — the anchor and, in most products, the record's identity
51: - title and description (fetched from the page automatically in many modern products, and user-editable everywhere)
52: - a preview thumbnail or icon
53: - organizational assignments: collections/folders and/or tags
54: - timestamps, favorite/pinned flags, and free-form notes in many products
55: 
56: Concept versus implementation — the core concepts are realized differently across products:
57: 
58: ```text
59: Concept:             Saved reference record
60: Implementations:     link with metadata (universal); record plus preserved page copy;
61:                      uploaded file kept as a library item (some products)
62: 
63: Concept:             User-controlled organization
64: Implementations:     hierarchical folders/collections; tags; favorites/pins;
65:                      manual ordering; an "unsorted" inbox for uncategorized saves
66: 
67: Concept:             Retrieval
68: Implementations:     search over titles/URLs/descriptions/tags (full-text over page
69:                      content in some products); browse by collection or tag; filters; sort
70: ```
71: 
72: ### Capabilities Shared by Mature Products
73: 
74: These are standard in current standalone products. They make the library practical but do not define the Type:
75: 
76: - **Capture machinery** — a browser extension or bookmarklet (save from any page without leaving it), a mobile share-sheet target, a manual "add URL" form, and bulk import from browsers or other services.
77: - **Metadata enrichment** — automatic extraction of title, description, and preview imagery from the saved page; editable by the user.
78: - **Layered organization** — nested collections/folders and/or tags, often both; favorites or pinned items; a landing zone (unsorted/inbox) for saves the user hasn't classified yet.
79: - **Retrieval machinery** — search across the library, filters (by tag, type, date), sorting (newest-first is the common default), and bulk edit tools for reorganizing at scale.
80: - **Multi-device, multi-browser access** — web, desktop, and mobile clients sharing one library; independence from any single browser profile is the reason standalone products exist.
81: - **Interoperability** — import/export in the standard browser-bookmark HTML format, which functions as the Type's interchange convention.
82: - **Library hygiene** — duplicate detection or prevention; awareness of broken links (detection or error listings). Common in standalone products, though depth varies.
83: - **Preservation copies** — a saved snapshot of the page (local file, vendor-hosted copy, or a third-party web archive) so the content survives even if the original disappears. 84: - **Private-first sharing** — the library defaults to private; sharing a single link, a collection, or the whole account is an explicit, optional act.
85: - **Read-later affordances** — unread flags, clean reader views, reminders. A common hybrid overlap with Read-it-later, not part of the definition.
86: 
87: ## How It Works
88: 
89: ### Capture
90: 
91: ```text
92: Encounter a page (in a browser or app)
93: → invoke the save surface (extension / share sheet / add form)
94: → the product creates a record: URL + fetched title, description, preview
95: → optionally pick a collection and add tags at save time
96: → done — the record is in the library
97: ```
98: 
99: Capture is designed to cost seconds. If the user skips classification, the record lands in an unsorted area to be triaged later. 100: 
101: ### Organize
102: 
103: ```text
104: Open the unsorted area (or any collection)
105: → assign records to collections, apply or clean up tags
106: → restructure: nest, rename, merge, or reorder collections
107: → bulk operations move or relabel many records at once
108: ```
109: 
110: Organization is retroactive and continuously editable — records can be re-filed at any time, and the organizational structure itself (unlike a file system) is usually cheap to reshape because records are small.
111: 
112: ### Find and return
113: 
114: ```text
115: Remember something about the record (a word, a tag, the topic)
116: → search, or browse to the collection/tag
117: → scan result list (newest-first, or filtered/sorted)
118: → open the record → click through to the live resource
119: ```
120: 
121: Retrieval is the loop the whole Type exists for. Results are the user's own records; the product finds things the user has already seen and chosen to keep — the inverse of a search engine, which finds things the user has never seen.
122: 
123: ### Maintain
124: 
125: ```text
126: Periodically: run duplicate review → merge or remove
127: → check broken-link reports → repair (find replacement) or delete
128: → optionally trigger/request preserved copies of important records
129: → deleted records go to a recoverable trash in some products
130: ```
131: 
132: Because the referenced content lives on the web and out of the application's control, maintenance is a permanent background concern of this Type — link rot is structural, not an edge case.
133: 
134: ## Interfaces
135:

137: 
138: The primary surface: the accumulated records in a browsable list.
139: 
140: - typical information: title, URL/source, thumbnail, tags, collection, date added
141: - primary actions: open record, edit, move, tag, favorite, delete, select-many for bulk actions
142: 
143: ### Capture surface
144: 
145: A small overlay, not a full screen: the browser-extension popup, the mobile share target, or the add form.
146: 
147: - typical information: page URL and fetched title/preview
148: - primary actions: save, pick collection, add tags, (sometimes) set reminder
149: 
150: ### Collection / organization sidebar
151: 
152: The library's structural map.
153: 
154: - typical information: collection tree (often nestable), tag list or cloud, special views (unsorted, favorites, trash)
155: - primary actions: create/rename/nest/merge/delete collections, browse into one
156: 
157: ### Record detail / edit
158: 
159: One record's full surface.
160: 
161: - typical information: URL, title, description, preview, notes, tags, collection, timestamps; sometimes the preserved copy or an embedded reader view
162: - primary actions: edit fields, move/recategorize, open original, preserve copy, delete
163: 
164: ### Search and filters
165: 
166: - typical information: query field, filter controls (tag, type, date), result list

170: 
171: Where deletions land in products that offer recovery; excluded from search and normal views until restored or purged.

1: # Bookmark Manager
2: 
3: A fast, modern, and privacy-focused bookmark manager built for the web. Organize, tag, and manage your links with a clean and responsive interface. All data is stored locally in your browser using IndexedDB, ensuring complete privacy and offline access.
4: 
5: This project is based on the [Bookmark Manager App challenge by Frontend Mentor](https://www.frontendmentor.io/challenges/bookmark-manager-app).
6: 
7: ## Preview
8: 
9: ![Homepage Preview](./preview.png)
10: 
11: ## Features
12: 
13: - **Local-First Storage**
14:   All bookmarks are stored securely in your browser using IndexedDB. No accounts, servers, or tracking.
15: 
16: - **Tagging System**
17:   Organize bookmarks with custom tags for quick filtering and discovery.
18: 
19: - **Smart Sorting**
20:   Sort bookmarks by recently added, recently visited, or most visited.
21: 
22: - **Archiving & Pinning**
23:   Archive old bookmarks to reduce clutter or pin important links to the top.
24: 
25: - **Responsive Design**
26:   Optimized for desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.
27: 
28: - **Dark Mode**
29:   Clean high-contrast dark theme powered by DaisyUI.
30: 
31: - **Fast & Reactive UI**
32:   Built with Ripple TS for minimal overhead and smooth interactions.
33: 
34: ## Tech Stack
35: 
36: Built using modern web technologies:
37: 
38: - **Framework:** Ripple TS
39: - **Build Tool:** Vite
40: - **Styling:** Tailwind CSS v4 + DaisyUI v5
41: - **Database:** Dexie.js (IndexedDB wrapper)
42: - **Validation:** Valibot
43: - **Package Manager:** Bun
44: 
45: ## Getting Started
46: 
47: ### Prerequisites
48: 
49: Ensure you have [Bun](https://bun.sh) installed on your system.
50: 
51: ### Installation
52: 
53: 1. Clone the repository:
54: 
55: ```bash
56: git clone https://github.com/LakhindarPal/bookmark-manager.git
57: ```
58: 
59: 2. Navigate to the project directory:
60: 
61: ```bash
62: cd bookmark-manager
63: ```
64: 
65: 3. Install dependencies:
66: 
67: ```bash
68: bun install
69: ```
70: 
71: ## Development
72: 
73: Start the local development server:
74: 
75: ```bash
76: bun dev
77: ```
78: 
79: The application will be available at:
80: 
81: ```txt
82: http://localhost:5173
83: ```
84: 
85: ## Production Build
86: 
87: Create an optimized production build:
88: 
89: ```bash
90: bun run build
91: ```
92: 
93: Compiled assets will be generated in the `dist` directory.
94: 
95: ## Code Quality
96: 
97: Format the codebase:
98: 
99: ```bash
100: bun format
101: ```
102: 
103: Run the linter:
104: 
105: ```bash
106: bun lint
107: ```
108: 
109: ## Contributing
110: 
111: Contributions, issues, and feature requests are welcome.
112: 
113: If you'd like to contribute:
114: 
115: 1. Fork the repository
116: 2. Create a feature branch
117: 3. Make your changes
118: 4. Ensure formatting and linting pass
119: 5. Open a pull request with a clear description of your changes
120:

1: # Bookmark Manager

4: 
5: This project is based on the [Bookmark Manager App challenge by Frontend Mentor](https://www.frontendmentor.io/challenges/bookmark-manager-app).

17:   Organize bookmarks with custom tags for quick filtering and discovery.
18: 
19: - **Smart Sorting**
20:   Sort bookmarks by recently added, recently visited, or most visited.
21: 
22: - **Archiving & Pinning**
23:   Archive old bookmarks to reduce clutter or pin important links to the top.
24:

27:
